idiom_name: party count (or completion count) + release condition + explicit abort/timeout policy
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: give each phase a rendezvous object created with an explicit party count; every participant performs its phase work, then arrives (increment and wait, or count down and wait) and the last arrival releases the generation. For one-shot fan-in, invert the roles: N producers signal completion on every exit path and one waiter blocks until the count reaches zero. In both forms the non-negotiable part is the failure contract: bind the wait with a timeout or cancellation signal and define what happens when a participant never arrives (abort or broken state propagated to every waiter, or an explicit error) - a rendezvous without that policy is a hang waiting for a trigger. Prefer the platform primitive over a hand-rolled counter; when the runtime's concurrency model cannot block, use the runtime's own construct instead of importing a blocking one.
code_sketch:
phase = Barrier(parties=N)            # reusable: auto-resets each generation
worker(i):
    for step in steps:
        compute(i, step)
        if phase.arrive_and_wait(timeout) is leader:
            merge_partials()             # exactly once per generation
# one-shot fan-in:
done = Latch(count=N)
producer(): try { work() } finally { done.count_down() }  # every exit path
done.wait(timeout); if timed_out: abort_group()
pitfalls: Declaring the rendezvous but not its failure policy: a participant that never arrives hangs the group with no diagnostic.
Party-count drift - participants added, removed or retried without adjusting the count - releasing early or never.
Awaiting the rendezvous on a resource the counted work also needs (a bounded pool, a lock, the event loop).
